source.title: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Minglai Yang; Xin-Yu Guo; Zheng-Liang Shi; Jin-He Bi; Steven Bethard; Mihai Surdeanu; Liangming Pan

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some equations and layout are imperfectly rendered, but the relevant content is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper motivates sparse autoencoders as a response to superposition and polysemantic neuron activity, then uses SAEs to build concept-aligned slots. Its experiments test SAE feature alignment and steering, not whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or why they do so.
record.gate_note: The introduction makes background statements about superposition and mixed neuron activity, but does not test them. The paper's own measurements concern SAE features rather than individual neurons. The MIG results below are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version; cited claims from prior work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper cites superposition and polysemantic neurons only as motivation for sparse autoencoders. Its experiments train concept-supervised SAEs on GPT-2 residual-stream activations. It reports binding, MIG, swap and steering results for SAE slots. It never measures whether individual neurons (MLP or vision) respond to unrelated inputs, or why. The only raw-activation analyses (Appendix E top-50 activations, Appendix H t-SNE) are qualitative views of residual-stream vectors, not neuron-level polysemanticity measures.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude that 'pre-train, then post-train' concept supervision binds ontology relations to dedicated SAE slots in frozen GPT-2, with best results at mid layers (Layer 6). These slots are more disentangled (MIG) and more causally controllable than standard SAE features: 1-hop swap success about 85–95%, but only 7.86% in 2-hop. The authors also use the slots to probe grokking-like dynamics. They draw no experimental conclusion about individual neurons.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised concept-aligned SAE training and slot interventions, rather than testing individual neuron responses with the methods in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports outcome changes across transformer layers and intervention strengths; for example, binding and swap control are strongest around Layer 6, and swap success varies with amplification strength.

fits_no_version.finding: A standard SAE has MIG 0.000 (1-hop) and 0.004 (2-hop) between features and relation labels. Concept-supervised AlignSAE slots reach 0.173 and 0.035. A standard SAE spreads each concept over hundreds to thousands of features (EffFeat), with Top1C ≈ 0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unsupervised SAE features on GPT-2 fragment human-defined relation concepts across many features. Concept-supervised post-training concentrates each concept into one slot.

record.peer_reviewed: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (published 08/2026, as stated in the text)
record.problems: The paper's experiments concern GPT-2 and controlled synthetic or templated tasks, not individual-neuron polysemanticity. The authors note that evaluation is limited to one architecture and synthetic data; the 2-hop swap success is 7.86% in absolute terms.

untested.parts: No vision models or vision neurons are studied.
No measurement of the share of GPT-2 MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, or of how that share varies by layer.
Superposition is asserted in the introduction from prior work and is not tested.
No experiments on polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
No variation of activation function, architecture or regularization with a neuron-level polysemanticity measure.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No analysis of how a neuron's polysemantic classification depends on activation range or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The tranche is between T4 and cites_only: the SAE method is motivated by polysemanticity and superposition, but the paper never checks them. All four rows are the study's own method compared with a baseline, at the SAE-feature level. A standard SAE's MIG of 0.000 shows distributed SAE features, not neuron polysemanticity.

versions.untested_parts: Whether individual neurons in vision models respond to unrelated image inputs.
Whether MLP neurons in transformer language models commonly respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how prevalence varies by layer.
Whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than available neurons and packing them together.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
Whether neuron polysemanticity varies by activation, architecture, or regularization, or can be reduced without substantial performance loss.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs, rather than unrelated mixtures.
Whether neuron polysemanticity depends on activation range examined or explanation-scoring method.
